152	
153	| Question | Answer | Source |
154	|---|---|---|
155	| **Does Gemma 4 do tool/function calling?** | **Yes, natively.** Gemma 4 lists "built-in function-calling support". The chat template has dedicated tool tokens (`<\|tool_call>call:name{…}<tool_call\|>`) | [Gemma 4 overview](https://ai.google.dev/gemma/docs/core); [Gemma function calling](https://ai.google.dev/gemma/docs/capabilities/function-calling) |
156	| …via the **Gemini API**? | **Yes.** The Gemini API "supports the following Gemma 4 models: `gemma-4-31b-it` and `gemma-4-26b-a4b-it`". Function declarations work as with Gemini ("The model decides when to call them"). System instructions are supported. **Structured output / JSON mode is not documented for Gemma** there | [Gemma on Gemini API](https://ai.google.dev/gemma/docs/core/gemma_on_gemini_api?hl=en) |
157	| …via **Ollama**? | **Yes.** The `gemma4` library page carries the **tools** badge. Tags: `e2b`, `e4b`, `12b`, `26b`, `31b` | [Ollama gemma4](https://ollama.com/library/gemma4) |
158	| …in a way **Mastra** can use? | **Probably, but unproven ⚠.** Mastra's model router lists `google/gemma-4-31b-it` and `google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it` (key `GOOGLE_API_KEY`), but its **Tools column for both is blank**. Mastra does not advertise tool support for them. Ollama works through an AI SDK community provider (`ollama-ai-provider-v2`). The AI SDK docs point to the alternative `ai-sdk-ollama` package for "reliable tool calling". A user reported Gemma 4 tool calls via Ollama not being recognised in **streaming** mode through the AI SDK OpenAI-compatible provider. **Decision:** use `generate()` (non-streaming). Run the 20-prompt smoke test at Gate 1 (§2.4). If validity is below 16/20, switch to the **prefetch fallback**: code runs the tools and Gemma only reasons and returns JSON. That keeps Gemma, Mastra and memory | [Mastra Google provider](https://mastra.ai/models/providers/google); [Mastra Ollama](https://mastra.ai/models/providers/ollama); [AI SDK Ollama](https://ai-sdk.dev/providers/community-providers/ollama); [OpenCode issue #20995](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues/20995) |
159	| Structured output with tools | Use `structuredOutput: { schema, jsonPromptInjection: true }`. Mastra documents that some models "can't combine structured output with tools". For Gemini 2.5 with tools, `jsonPromptInjection: true` is required. Assume the same for Gemma. Read `response.object` | [Mastra structured output](https://mastra.ai/docs/agents/structured-output) |
160	| Mastra agent API | `new Agent({ id, name, instructions, model: 'provider/model', tools, memory })` from `@mastra/core/agent`. `createTool({ id, description, inputSchema, outputSchema, execute: async (input, ctx) => … })` from `@mastra/core/tools`. `agent.generate(msg, { memory: { resource, thread }, maxSteps, structuredOutput, toolChoice })` returns `text, object, toolCalls, toolResults, steps, usage` | [Agents](https://mastra.ai/docs/agents/overview); [createTool](https://mastra.ai/reference/tools/create-tool); [generate()](https://mastra.ai/reference/agents/generate) |
161	| Mastra memory on MongoDB | `@mastra/mongodb` provides `MongoDBStore({ id, uri, dbName })` and `MongoDBVector({ id, uri, dbName })`. Semantic recall = `options.semanticRecall: { topK, messageRange, scope: 'resource' }` plus `vector` and `embedder`. MongoDB supports `scope: 'resource'`. Working memory exists but is updated through an `updateWorkingMemory` **tool call**. Quorum therefore keeps the roster in its own collection, so roster updates don't depend on Gemma tool calls | [MongoDB storage](https://mastra.ai/reference/storage/mongodb); [MongoDB vector](https://mastra.ai/reference/vectors/mongodb); [Semantic recall](https://mastra.ai/docs/memory/semantic-recall); [Working memory](https://mastra.ai/docs/memory/working-memory) |
162	| Mastra server on Render | `mastra build` → `.mastra/output/index.mjs`. Start with `node .mastra/output/index.mjs`. `PORT` overrides 4111. **Host defaults to `localhost`**, so set `MASTRA_HOST=0.0.0.0` on Render. `GET /health` returns 200. Custom routes via `registerApiRoute` from `@mastra/core/server`; handlers get a Hono context with `c.get('mastra')` | [Mastra server](https://mastra.ai/docs/deployment/mastra-server); [Config](https://mastra.ai/reference/configuration); [Custom routes](https://mastra.ai/docs/server/custom-api-routes) |
163	| Temporal timers | `sleep('5s')`, `sleep(ms)`. "Timers are persisted, so even if your Worker or Temporal Service is down…" the sleep resolves when they're back. `condition(fn, timeout)` returns false on timeout | [TS timers](https://docs.temporal.io/develop/typescript/timers) |
164	| Temporal signals/queries | `wf.defineSignal('x')`, `wf.defineQuery<T>('y')`, `wf.setHandler(...)`. Client: `handle.signal(sig, arg)` and `client.workflow.signalWithStart(...)` | [TS message passing](https://docs.temporal.io/develop/typescript/message-passing) |
165	| Temporal activity retries | Activities retry by default: initial 1 s, backoff 2.0, max interval 100× initial, **unlimited attempts**, no non-retryable errors. "Workflow Executions do not retry by default." **Each retry is NOT written to event history.** You see attempt count and last failure in the UI's *Pending Activities* panel while it retries, then one `ActivityTaskStarted` with `attempt: N` and `lastFailure`. To keep every attempt, log it yourself (Quorum writes each attempt to `plans.events`) | [Retry policies](https://docs.temporal.io/encyclopedia/retry-policies); [Temporal forum](https://community.temporal.io/t/how-to-save-all-retry-attempt-failure-logs/14903) |
166	| Temporal persistence | `temporal server start-dev --db-filename quorum.db`. "By default, Workflow Executions are lost when the server process dies." UI = `--port` + 1000 = 8233 | [Temporal CLI](https://docs.temporal.io/cli/server) |
167	| Render Free limits | Spins down after "15 minutes without receiving any inbound traffic". Spin-up "takes about one minute". Ephemeral filesystem. 750 instance-hours/month. No outbound SMTP ports. Only web services, Postgres and Key Value are Free (**no free background workers**). Free web service: 512 MB, <1 CPU | [Render Free](https://render.com/docs/free); [Render pricing](https://render.com/pricing) |
168	| Atlas M0 Vector Search | Available on M0. **Max 3 search + vector indexes in total.** 0.5 GB storage, 100 ops/s, 500 connections. Mastra's MongoDB storage needs an instance "with MongoDB Search enabled", and MongoDB 7.0+ is recommended (Atlas M0 qualifies; inferred) | [VS limitations](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/deployment/compatibility-limitations/); [M0 limits](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/free-shared-limitations/); [Mastra MongoDB](https://mastra.ai/reference/storage/mongodb) |

Secrets are redacted before anything leaves your machine. CLI is MIT | [Quickstart](https://docs.entire.io/quickstart.md); [Storage](https://docs.entire.io/guides/checkpoints/checkpoint-storage.md); [Inspect in CLI](https://docs.entire.io/guides/checkpoints/inspect-in-cli.md); [Search in CLI](https://docs.entire.io/guides/search/search-in-cli.md); [docs.entire.io](https://docs.entire.io) |

177	## 2.3 Architecture, data model, repo layout
178	
179	### Architecture (text diagram)
180	
181	```
182	 ┌────────────── Telegram group (the real friends) ───────────────┐
183	 │ /join  /me <constraint>  /plan  poll taps  replies w/ photo     │
184	 └───────▲──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
185	         │ sendMessage/sendPoll         │ getUpdates (long poll, privacy mode ON)
186	         │ (activities)                 ▼
187	 ┌───────┴───────────── YOUR LAPTOP (stays awake Sat→Sun) ───────────────────┐
188	 │  bot.ts ──signal(vote|recap)/start──► Temporal dev server (quorum.db, :8233)│
189	 │                                          │ tasks                            │
190	 │                                   worker.ts ── activities: draftPlans,      │
191	 │                                          │     recheckWeather, storeRecap,  │
192	 │                                          │     sendPoll, say, savePlan      │
193	 └──────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┘
194	                     HTTPS + shared secret  │  (25 s timeout → retried by Temporal;
195	                                            ▼   Render cold start = a real flaky call)
196	 ┌──────────── RENDER FREE WEB SERVICE (sleeps after 15 min) ─────────────┐
197	 │ Mastra server: agent "quorum" (Gemma 4 via Gemini API)                 │
198	 │   tools: weather (Open-Meteo), places (Overpass), liveCheck (SerpApi*) │
199	 │ routes: /quorum/draft  /quorum/recheck  /quorum/remember               │
200	 │         /p/:planId (public plan page)  /try (judge demo)  /health      │
201	 └────────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
202	                                      ▼
203	 ┌──────────── MONGODB ATLAS M0 ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
204	 │ Mastra: threads/messages + vector index (semantic recall, 768-d)        │
205	 │ App: members · plans · polls · recaps · serp_cache                      │
206	 └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
207	```
208	
209	For the **post**, redraw it with 5 boxes: Telegram → Laptop (Temporal + worker + bot) → Render (Mastra + Gemma) → Atlas, with Open-Meteo/OSM as a side box. The persuasion rule allows no more than 6 boxes.
210	
211	**Who owns what (say this in the post):** Temporal owns **time** (waiting, retrying, reminding). Mastra owns **reasoning** (which plan, why). Atlas owns **memory** (who can't do what, what happened last time). Render owns the **public face** (the agent API, the plan page, the judge demo). The laptop holds only the clock and the bot token.
212	
213	### MongoDB schema (database `quorum`)
214	
215	```ts
216	// members: one doc per person who /join'ed. _id = `${chatId}:${userId}`
217	{ _id, chatId, userId, name, consentAt: Date,
218	  constraints: [{ text: "knee hates long descents", addedAt: Date }] }
219	// plans: one doc per workflow. _id = workflowId = `plan-${chatId}-${date}`
220	{ _id, chatId, date, quorum, status: 'drafting'|'voting'|'locked'|'no-quorum'|'fallback'|'reminded'|'recap'|'done',
221	  options: [{ title, where, start, durationH, shapedBy: [string], weatherNote }],
222	  counts: [number], chosen?: {...}, weather?: { checkedAt, maxRain, go },
223	  events: [{ at: Date, type: string, detail: string }] }   // incl. every activity attempt
224	// polls: { _id: telegramPollId, planId, messageId }
225	// recaps: { _id, planId, chatId, userId, name, line, photoFileId?, at }
226	// serp_cache: { _id: sha1(query), query, results, fetchedAt }   (TTL index 12 h)
227	// mastra_* collections + vector index: created by @mastra/mongodb (1 of your 3 M0 indexes)
228	```
229	
230	Privacy rules (put them in the README): only people who `/join` are stored. `/forget` deletes your member doc. The public plan page shows **first names only, with consent**, or just counts. Photos stay as Telegram `file_id`s and are never re-hosted.
231	
232	### Repo layout
233	
234	```
235	quorum/
236	├── AGENTS.md  memory.md  README.md  LICENSE (Apache-2.0)
237	├── .github/copilot-instructions.md   .env.example   .gitignore   .entire/
238	├── render.yaml  package.json  tsconfig.json
239	├── src/
240	│   ├── mastra/
241	│   │   ├── index.ts              # Mastra instance (Render entry)
242	│   │   ├── agents/quorum.ts      # agent + no-tools twin (prefetch fallback)
243	│   │   ├── tools/weather.ts  places.ts  liveCheck.ts
244	│   │   ├── memory.ts             # MongoDBStore + MongoDBVector + embedder
245	│   │   └── routes.ts             # /quorum/*, /p/:id, /try, /
246	│   ├── shared/  db.ts  schema.ts  model.ts  time.ts
247	│   ├── temporal/ workflows.ts (FROZEN at real run)  activities.ts  worker.ts
248	│   └── bot/telegram.ts
249	├── scripts/ smoke-gemma.ts  run-local.sh
250	└── docs/evidence/               # screenshots for the post (no secrets)
251	```
252

308	`entire enable` makes the first commit if the folder is new, and creates `.entire/settings.json`. When Entire asks to link a commit to the agent session, answer **`a` (always)** ([quickstart](https://docs.entire.io/quickstart.md)).

318	   one real outing; a Temporal workflow holds the clock (poll, quorum deadline, 05:30
319	   weather re-check, 06:00 reminder, recap); memory in MongoDB Atlas; hosted on Render."

321	   - Read memory.md FIRST every task; UPDATE it LAST (summarize, don't dump — minimize tokens).
322	   - Edit only relevant files; don't scan the whole repo.
323	   - For any web UI, use the frontend-design skill.
324	   - After each working increment, git commit using Conventional Commits
325	     (feat/fix/docs/chore/refactor).
326	   - Keep README run steps current; secrets only in .env (git-ignored).
327	   - Ask before large refactors or heavy new dependencies.
328	   - QUORUM RULES: never edit src/temporal/workflows.ts after git tag `real-run-start`
329	     (Temporal determinism) — use wf.patched() or a new workflow type instead.
330	     Use agent.generate (never stream) with Gemma. Every external call in an activity
331	     has an explicit AbortSignal.timeout. Never invent place names: only tool output.
332	     Store only /join'ed members; /forget deletes. No human co-authors in commits.
333	3. Create .github/copilot-instructions.md pointing to AGENTS.md.
334	4. Create README.md (stub: what it is + how to run), LICENSE (Apache-2.0), .env.example
335	   (GOOGLE_API_KEY, MONGODB_URI, MONGODB_DB, TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN, RENDER_URL,
336	   QUORUM_SHARED_SECRET, QUORUM_MODEL, TOOL_MODE, GROUP_UTC_OFFSET, HOME_LAT, HOME_LON,
337	   SERPAPI_KEY), .gitignore (node_modules, .env, .temporal/, .mastra/).
338	5. Commit: "chore: bootstrap project + agent workflow".
339	
340	Then stop and show me memory.md and AGENTS.md before building features.
341	```

# PART II — BUILD PHASE

## 2.0 Pre-flight (do these before Hour 0; ~45 min, can overlap)

**People first.** The binding constraint is your friends, not code. **Right now**, before you open an editor, message your group:

> "Experiment this weekend: I'm building a bot that plans one short outing for us and nags us so it actually happens. Sunday morning, 2–3 hours, close by. Can you do Sunday morning? If yes, I'll add you to a Telegram group tonight. It only reads messages you send *to it* (commands/replies), and you can `/forget` yourself any time."

Then export your existing group chat (WhatsApp: *More → Export chat → Without media*; Telegram Desktop: *Export chat history*). Count the real phrase:

```bash
grep -ciE "we should|let'?s (go|do|plan)" chat.txt   # → {{WE_SHOULD_COUNT}}
grep -iE "we should" chat.txt | head -1               # first date → {{SINCE_DATE}}
```

Ask the group whether you may quote that number and two of their messages. Then create the accounts, verifying "no card" on each:

| # | Account / install | Card? | Verified source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | GitHub repo `quorum` (public, **Apache-2.0**) | No | — |
| 2 | Google AI Studio API key (`GOOGLE_API_KEY`). Gemma 4 is "Free of charge"; Paid Tier "Not available" | No (free tier) | [Gemini pricing](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing) |
| 3 | MongoDB Atlas **M0** cluster, a DB user, Network Access `0.0.0.0/0` (Render has no static IP on Free) | Not stated on the official page. Stop if asked | [M0 limits](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/free-shared-limitations/) |
| 4 | Render account (GitHub login), Free web service | No ("If you haven't added a payment method…") | [Render Free](https://render.com/docs/free) |
| 5 | Telegram bot via **@BotFather** `/newbot` → `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN`. **Leave privacy mode ON** | No | [Telegram privacy mode](https://core.telegram.org/bots/features#privacy-mode) |
| 6 | Temporal CLI (`brew install temporal`, or the Linux/Windows binary from the Temporal CLI docs) | No (OSS) | [Temporal CLI server](https://docs.temporal.io/cli/server) |
| 7 | Entire CLI: `curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh \| bash` (macOS: `brew install --cask entireio/tap/entire`) | No (MIT) | [Entire quickstart](https://docs.entire.io/quickstart.md) |
| 8 | Node 22 LTS, `npm`, optionally Ollama + `ollama pull gemma4:e4b` (6.6–9.5 GB) for the local comparison | No | [Ollama gemma4](https://ollama.com/library/gemma4) |
| 9 | *(stretch)* SerpApi key. Free = 250 searches/month, 50/hour | Not stated. Stop if asked | [SerpApi pricing](https://serpapi.com/pricing) |
| 10 | Promos: log in at [hacktoberfest.com/my/promos](https://hacktoberfest.com/my/promos) and claim the Render promo if one is offered. Not required; Free tier suffices | — | [Challenge page](https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-week1-2026-10-05) |

**Fallback decision made up front:** if Atlas asks for a card → §2.6 "Atlas". If Render asks for a card → §2.6 "Render". If neither asks, proceed.

## 2.1 Stack

| Layer | Choice | Why (and why not the alternative) |
|---|---|---|
| Language | TypeScript, Node 22 | Mastra and the Temporal TS SDK are both TypeScript-native. One language for agent, workflow and bot |
| Agent framework | **Mastra** (`@mastra/core`, `@mastra/memory`, `@mastra/mongodb`), Apache-2.0 | Agents, tools, memory and an HTTP server in one package ([Mastra agents](https://mastra.ai/docs/agents/overview); [pricing/licence](https://mastra.ai/pricing)). Not LangChain: no first-class MongoDB memory with semantic recall in one config object |
| Model | **Gemma 4**: `google/gemma-4-31b-it` via the Gemini API free tier; `gemma4:e4b` via Ollama locally | Open weights, $0, and the same agent swaps to local. Gemma 4 has "built-in function-calling support" ([Gemma 4 overview](https://ai.google.dev/gemma/docs/core)). Not a closed API: the group's private facts would have no local option |
| Durability | **Temporal** OSS dev server + TS worker on your laptop | `temporal server start-dev --db-filename …` persists state; the Web UI is at :8233 ([Temporal CLI](https://docs.temporal.io/cli/server)). Not Temporal Cloud (needs a card, [pricing](https://temporal.io/pricing)). Not cron/`setTimeout` (dies on restart) |
| Memory / DB | **MongoDB Atlas M0** (512 MB, 100 ops/s, 500 connections, **max 3 search/vector indexes**) | [M0 limits](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/free-shared-limitations/); "3 indexes (regardless of the type, `search` or `vector`) on Free clusters" ([Vector Search limitations](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/deployment/compatibility-limitations/)) |
| Embeddings | `google/gemini-embedding-001` (768-d) via Mastra's `ModelRouterEmbeddingModel` | [Mastra embeddings](https://mastra.ai/models/embeddings). Same key as Gemma. Fallback: `@mastra/fastembed` (local) |
| Host | **Render Free web service** running `mastra build` output | The only host that is also a prize category. Free sleeps after 15 idle min and takes ~1 min to wake ([Render Free](https://render.com/docs/free)), which the design turns into a feature |
| Chat channel | **Telegram Bot API**, long polling from your laptop | Free and instant (BotFather), no public webhook or tunnel needed (`getUpdates` long polling), and native non-anonymous polls send per-voter `poll_answer` updates. Privacy mode means the bot only sees commands and replies addressed to it ([Bot API](https://core.telegram.org/bots/api)). Discord would also work (free) but needs a gateway client and has no per-voter poll update as simple as this. WhatsApp is out (business verification, paid) |
| Weather | Open-Meteo (no key; free for non-commercial use; 10,000 calls/day) | [Open-Meteo pricing](https://open-meteo.com/en/pricing) |
| Places | OSM Overpass API (public instance: ~10,000 requests/day, <1 GB/day) | [Overpass commons](https://dev.overpass-api.de/overpass-doc/en/preface/commons.html) |
| Live check *(stretch)* | SerpApi Google engine, cached in Atlas | [SerpApi pricing](https://serpapi.com/pricing) |
| Session history | **Entire CLI** with the **branch** checkpoint backend | Judges can browse `entire/checkpoints/v1` on GitHub without an Entire account (inferred; see §2.2) |

## 2.2 Verified build facts and the report's open questions, resolved

Checked against primary docs on 2026-10-09. ⚠ = not verified end-to-end. Your Hour-2 gate tests it.

| Question | Answer | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **Does Gemma 4 do tool/function calling?** | **Yes, natively.** Gemma 4 lists "built-in function-calling support". The chat template has dedicated tool tokens (`<\|tool_call>call:name{…}<tool_call\|>`) | [Gemma 4 overview](https://ai.google.dev/gemma/docs/core); [Gemma function calling](https://ai.google.dev/gemma/docs/capabilities/function-calling) |
| …via the **Gemini API**? | **Yes.** The Gemini API "supports the following Gemma 4 models: `gemma-4-31b-it` and `gemma-4-26b-a4b-it`". Function declarations work as with Gemini ("The model decides when to call them"). System instructions are supported. **Structured output / JSON mode is not documented for Gemma** there | [Gemma on Gemini API](https://ai.google.dev/gemma/docs/core/gemma_on_gemini_api?hl=en) |
| …via **Ollama**? | **Yes.** The `gemma4` library page carries the **tools** badge. Tags: `e2b`, `e4b`, `12b`, `26b`, `31b` | [Ollama gemma4](https://ollama.com/library/gemma4) |
| …in a way **Mastra** can use? | **Probably, but unproven ⚠.** Mastra's model router lists `google/gemma-4-31b-it` and `google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it` (key `GOOGLE_API_KEY`), but its **Tools column for both is blank**. Mastra does not advertise tool support for them. Ollama works through an AI SDK community provider (`ollama-ai-provider-v2`). The AI SDK docs point to the alternative `ai-sdk-ollama` package for "reliable tool calling". A user reported Gemma 4 tool calls via Ollama not being recognised in **streaming** mode through the AI SDK OpenAI-compatible provider. **Decision:** use `generate()` (non-streaming). Run the 20-prompt smoke test at Gate 1 (§2.4). If validity is below 16/20, switch to the **prefetch fallback**: code runs the tools and Gemma only reasons and returns JSON. That keeps Gemma, Mastra and memory | [Mastra Google provider](https://mastra.ai/models/providers/google); [Mastra Ollama](https://mastra.ai/models/providers/ollama); [AI SDK Ollama](https://ai-sdk.dev/providers/community-providers/ollama); [OpenCode issue #20995](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues/20995) |
| Structured output with tools | Use `structuredOutput: { schema, jsonPromptInjection: true }`. Mastra documents that some models "can't combine structured output with tools". For Gemini 2.5 with tools, `jsonPromptInjection: true` is required. Assume the same for Gemma. Read `response.object` | [Mastra structured output](https://mastra.ai/docs/agents/structured-output) |
| Mastra agent API | `new Agent({ id, name, instructions, model: 'provider/model', tools, memory })` from `@mastra/core/agent`. `createTool({ id, description, inputSchema, outputSchema, execute: async (input, ctx) => … })` from `@mastra/core/tools`. `agent.generate(msg, { memory: { resource, thread }, maxSteps, structuredOutput, toolChoice })` returns `text, object, toolCalls, toolResults, steps, usage` | [Agents](https://mastra.ai/docs/agents/overview); [createTool](https://mastra.ai/reference/tools/create-tool); [generate()](https://mastra.ai/reference/agents/generate) |
| Mastra memory on MongoDB | `@mastra/mongodb` provides `MongoDBStore({ id, uri, dbName })` and `MongoDBVector({ id, uri, dbName })`. Semantic recall = `options.semanticRecall: { topK, messageRange, scope: 'resource' }` plus `vector` and `embedder`. MongoDB supports `scope: 'resource'`. Working memory exists but is updated through an `updateWorkingMemory` **tool call**. Quorum therefore keeps the roster in its own collection, so roster updates don't depend on Gemma tool calls | [MongoDB storage](https://mastra.ai/reference/storage/mongodb); [MongoDB vector](https://mastra.ai/reference/vectors/mongodb); [Semantic recall](https://mastra.ai/docs/memory/semantic-recall); [Working memory](https://mastra.ai/docs/memory/working-memory) |
| Mastra server on Render | `mastra build` → `.mastra/output/index.mjs`. Start with `node .mastra/output/index.mjs`. `PORT` overrides 4111. **Host defaults to `localhost`**, so set `MASTRA_HOST=0.0.0.0` on Render. `GET /health` returns 200. Custom routes via `registerApiRoute` from `@mastra/core/server`; handlers get a Hono context with `c.get('mastra')` | [Mastra server](https://mastra.ai/docs/deployment/mastra-server); [Config](https://mastra.ai/reference/configuration); [Custom routes](https://mastra.ai/docs/server/custom-api-routes) |
| Temporal timers | `sleep('5s')`, `sleep(ms)`. "Timers are persisted, so even if your Worker or Temporal Service is down…" the sleep resolves when they're back. `condition(fn, timeout)` returns false on timeout | [TS timers](https://docs.temporal.io/develop/typescript/timers) |
| Temporal signals/queries | `wf.defineSignal('x')`, `wf.defineQuery<T>('y')`, `wf.setHandler(...)`. Client: `handle.signal(sig, arg)` and `client.workflow.signalWithStart(...)` | [TS message passing](https://docs.temporal.io/develop/typescript/message-passing) |
| Temporal activity retries | Activities retry by default: initial 1 s, backoff 2.0, max interval 100× initial, **unlimited attempts**, no non-retryable errors. "Workflow Executions do not retry by default." **Each retry is NOT written to event history.** You see attempt count and last failure in the UI's *Pending Activities* panel while it retries, then one `ActivityTaskStarted` with `attempt: N` and `lastFailure`. To keep every attempt, log it yourself (Quorum writes each attempt to `plans.events`) | [Retry policies](https://docs.temporal.io/encyclopedia/retry-policies); [Temporal forum](https://community.temporal.io/t/how-to-save-all-retry-attempt-failure-logs/14903) |
| Temporal persistence | `temporal server start-dev --db-filename quorum.db`. "By default, Workflow Executions are lost when the server process dies." UI = `--port` + 1000 = 8233 | [Temporal CLI](https://docs.temporal.io/cli/server) |
| Render Free limits | Spins down after "15 minutes without receiving any inbound traffic". Spin-up "takes about one minute". Ephemeral filesystem. 750 instance-hours/month. No outbound SMTP ports. Only web services, Postgres and Key Value are Free (**no free background workers**). Free web service: 512 MB, <1 CPU | [Render Free](https://render.com/docs/free); [Render pricing](https://render.com/pricing) |
| Atlas M0 Vector Search | Available on M0. **Max 3 search + vector indexes in total.** 0.5 GB storage, 100 ops/s, 500 connections. Mastra's MongoDB storage needs an instance "with MongoDB Search enabled", and MongoDB 7.0+ is recommended (Atlas M0 qualifies; inferred) | [VS limitations](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/deployment/compatibility-limitations/); [M0 limits](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/free-shared-limitations/); [Mastra MongoDB](https://mastra.ai/reference/storage/mongodb) |
| Entire CLI usage | `entire enable -y --agent <claude-code\|codex\|copilot-cli\|cursor\|opencode\|…>` installs hooks. On commit it asks to link the session, so answer `[a]lways`. `entire checkpoint list`, `entire checkpoint explain <commit>` (`--full`, `--short`), `entire search "…"` (needs `entire login`, searches **pushed** content). Checkpoints live in your repo. The default backend since 0.10.0 is refs (`refs/entire/checkpoints/…`), and `--checkpoint-backend branch` uses the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch. Secrets are redacted before anything leaves your machine. CLI is MIT | [Quickstart](https://docs.entire.io/quickstart.md); [Storage](https://docs.entire.io/guides/checkpoints/checkpoint-storage.md); [Inspect in CLI](https://docs.entire.io/guides/checkpoints/inspect-in-cli.md); [Search in CLI](https://docs.entire.io/guides/search/search-in-cli.md); [docs.entire.io](https://docs.entire.io) |

## 2.3 Architecture, data model, repo layout

### Architecture (text diagram)

```
 ┌────────────── Telegram group (the real friends) ───────────────┐
 │ /join  /me <constraint>  /plan  poll taps  replies w/ photo     │
 └───────▲──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
         │ sendMessage/sendPoll         │ getUpdates (long poll, privacy mode ON)
         │ (activities)                 ▼
 ┌───────┴───────────── YOUR LAPTOP (stays awake Sat→Sun) ───────────────────┐
 │  bot.ts ──signal(vote|recap)/start──► Temporal dev server (quorum.db, :8233)│
 │                                          │ tasks                            │
 │                                   worker.ts ── activities: draftPlans,      │
 │                                          │     recheckWeather, storeRecap,  │
 │                                          │     sendPoll, say, savePlan      │
 └──────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┘
                     HTTPS + shared secret  │  (25 s timeout → retried by Temporal;
                                            ▼   Render cold start = a real flaky call)
 ┌──────────── RENDER FREE WEB SERVICE (sleeps after 15 min) ─────────────┐
 │ Mastra server: agent "quorum" (Gemma 4 via Gemini API)                 │
 │   tools: weather (Open-Meteo), places (Overpass), liveCheck (SerpApi*) │
 │ routes: /quorum/draft  /quorum/recheck  /quorum/remember               │
 │         /p/:planId (public plan page)  /try (judge demo)  /health      │
 └────────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                                      ▼
 ┌──────────── MONGODB ATLAS M0 ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ Mastra: threads/messages + vector index (semantic recall, 768-d)        │
 │ App: members · plans · polls · recaps · serp_cache                      │
 └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

For the **post**, redraw it with 5 boxes: Telegram → Laptop (Temporal + worker + bot) → Render (Mastra + Gemma) → Atlas, with Open-Meteo/OSM as a side box. The persuasion rule allows no more than 6 boxes.

**Who owns what (say this in the post):** Temporal owns **time** (waiting, retrying, reminding). Mastra owns **reasoning** (which plan, why). Atlas owns **memory** (who can't do what, what happened last time). Render owns the **public face** (the agent API, the plan page, the judge demo). The laptop holds only the clock and the bot token.

### MongoDB schema (database `quorum`)

```ts
// members: one doc per person who /join'ed. _id = `${chatId}:${userId}`
{ _id, chatId, userId, name, consentAt: Date,
  constraints: [{ text: "knee hates long descents", addedAt: Date }] }
// plans: one doc per workflow. _id = workflowId = `plan-${chatId}-${date}`
{ _id, chatId, date, quorum, status: 'drafting'|'voting'|'locked'|'no-quorum'|'fallback'|'reminded'|'recap'|'done',
  options: [{ title, where, start, durationH, shapedBy: [string], weatherNote }],
  counts: [number], chosen?: {...}, weather?: { checkedAt, maxRain, go },
  events: [{ at: Date, type: string, detail: string }] }   // incl. every activity attempt
// polls: { _id: telegramPollId, planId, messageId }
// recaps: { _id, planId, chatId, userId, name, line, photoFileId?, at }
// serp_cache: { _id: sha1(query), query, results, fetchedAt }   (TTL index 12 h)
// mastra_* collections + vector index: created by @mastra/mongodb (1 of your 3 M0 indexes)
```

Privacy rules (put them in the README): only people who `/join` are stored. `/forget` deletes your member doc. The public plan page shows **first names only, with consent**, or just counts. Photos stay as Telegram `file_id`s and are never re-hosted.

### Hour 0 — Project bootstrap (vibecoding flow): ALWAYS FIRST

This step embeds the standard bootstrap from `vibecoding-bootstrap.md`. Do it **before any feature code**. Order matters, because Entire must be enabled **before** your first agent session so every session is captured.

```bash
mkdir quorum && cd quorum
git init && git config user.name "<YOUR NAME>" && git config user.email "<YOUR EMAIL>"
entire enable -y --agent <claude-code|codex|copilot-cli|cursor|opencode> --checkpoint-backend branch
gh repo create quorum --public --source . --push     # or create on github.com and add the remote
```

`entire enable` makes the first commit if the folder is new, and creates `.entire/settings.json`. When Entire asks to link a commit to the agent session, answer **`a` (always)** ([quickstart](https://docs.entire.io/quickstart.md)).

Then paste this **kickoff prompt** into your coding agent. It is the bootstrap's standard prompt with Quorum-specific rules added:

```
2. Create AGENTS.md with these rules:

     has an explicit AbortSignal.timeout. Never invent place names: only tool output.
     Store only /join'ed members; /forget deletes. No human co-authors in commits.
3. Create .github/copilot-instructions.md pointing to AGENTS.md.
4. Create README.md (stub: what it is + how to run), LICENSE (Apache-2.0), .env.example

```

# Frontend Design

Approach this as the design lead at a design studio known for giving every client a distinct visual identity that is not mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt cliché or templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk if justified.

## Ground your designs in the subject matter

If the brief does not identify what the product or subject matter is, identify it yourself before designing, and confirm with the client. You can come up with one concrete subject, the design's audience, and the design's primary job, as a proposal. If there's any information in your memory about the client's preferences or context about what they're building, use that as a hint. The subject's industry, subject matter, materials, and vernacular are where distinctive visual choices come from — a design for a toy for girls aged 8–11 will be very aesthetically different from a dashboard for financial analysts. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.

## Design principles

For web designs, the hero is the first thing viewers will see. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in the form that is most appropriate: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment, or other treatments. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the default treatment, so only use it if that's truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. You don't need a different typeface for display or headline text and body content: use one family or two, and if two, make them clearly distinct.

Choose your typefaces deliberately, not the default families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale following the default guidance of The Elements of Typographic Style with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. When type is used as a headline or visual element, use the type treatment itself as an active part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.

Default to line lengths of less than 80 characters. Serif typefaces can have slightly longer line lengths; give serif body text slightly more line-height than a sans-serif.

Avoid these default typographic treatments; they are the commonest tells of a generated page:
- Accenting just a single word or phrase in a headline, like putting one word in italic/bold or a different color.
- Using all caps for labels.
- Adding unnecessary typographic labels above content.

Visual structure is information. Structural devices like outlines, borders, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, etc., encode useful information about the content rather than decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence — like a stepped process or a timeline. Before adding numbered markers, check the content really is a sequence.

Use non-user-triggered motion sparingly and deliberately, only to draw attention. A single orchestrated moment — one page-load sequence or one reveal — lands better than scattered effects; fade-and-slide-up entrances on each section and hover transitions on every card are the generic default and read as AI-generated. Motion that answers a person's action (opening, expanding, confirming) is welcome when it shows what changed.

Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy and placeholder content. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.

## Process: plan, review against the brief, build, critique

For calibration, AI-generated design right now clusters around some traits:
1. a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta or warm-clay accent (often near #D97757 — Anthropic's own Claude-interaction accent, so on a user's brief it reads as a tell);
2. a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent;
3. a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns;
4. the SaaS-card kit: content chopped into identical rounded cards, one border-radius on everything regardless of hierarchy, the same soft grey shadow (rgba(0,0,0,.1)) under each, and gradient washes as decoration;
5. template chrome that appears whatever the subject: a tracked-out ALL-CAPS eyebrow label above every heading; meta strings joined with middle dots ('A · B · C'); labels built as 'WORD — fragment' with a spaced em dash; tinted near-black (#0B0B0B, #111) standing in for black; a monospace face for small data labels; a '→' appended to link and button text.

All traits are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. As with a hired human designer, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the client's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and principles.
- Color: describe the core base palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- Type: the typefaces and their roles.
- Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Include alignment guidance; should the content be left aligned, center aligned, justified?
- Principles: the high-level guidance for what makes this page unique.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and an element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with padding/margin between sections.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let one element be the memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected, visually accessible, harmonious color palettes. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots to review if your environment supports it — a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creatives have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand and use. They are design content, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality and minimalism to copywriting that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's perspective. Name things by what users will understand in simple language, not by how the system is built. A user manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something is or does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific and legible to new users is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A CTA says exactly what happens when it is used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the tone conversational: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each written element do exactly one job.

# Claude in Chrome browser automation

You have access to browser automation tools (mcp__claude-in-chrome__*) for interacting with web pages in Chrome. Follow these guidelines for effective browser automation.

## Loading deferred tools

If the mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load every tool you expect to need in ONE ToolSearch call — the select query accepts a comma-separated list — never one call per tool. Start with the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting.

## GIF recording

When performing multi-step browser interactions that the user may want to review or share, use mcp__claude-in-chrome__gif_creator to record them.

You must ALWAYS:
* Capture extra frames before and after taking actions to ensure smooth playback
* Name the file meaningfully to help the user identify it later (e.g., "login_process.gif")

## Console log debugging

You can use mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages to read console output. Console output may be verbose. If you are looking for specific log entries, use the 'pattern' parameter with a regex-compatible pattern. This filters results efficiently and avoids overwhelming output. For example, use pattern: "[MyApp]" to filter for application-specific logs rather than reading all console output.

## Alerts and dialogs

IMPORTANT: Do not trigger JavaScript alerts, confirms, prompts, or browser modal dialogs through your actions. These browser dialogs block all further browser events and will prevent the extension from receiving any subsequent commands. Instead, when possible, use console.log for debugging and then use the mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages tool to read those log messages. If a page has dialog-triggering elements:
1. Avoid clicking buttons or links that may trigger alerts (e.g., "Delete" buttons with confirmation dialogs)
2. If you must interact with such elements, warn the user first that this may interrupt the session
3. Use mcp__claude-in-chrome__javascript_tool to check for and dismiss any existing dialogs before proceeding

If you accidentally trigger a dialog and lose responsiveness, inform the user they need to manually dismiss it in the browser.

## Avoid rabbit holes and loops

When using browser automation tools, stay focused on the specific task. If you encounter any of the following, stop and ask the user for guidance:
- Unexpected complexity or tangential browser exploration
- Browser tool calls failing or returning errors after 2-3 attempts
- No response from the browser extension
- Page elements not responding to clicks or input
- Pages not loading or timing out
- Unable to complete the browser task despite multiple approaches

Explain what you attempted, what went wrong, and ask how the user would like to proceed. Do not keep retrying the same failing browser action or explore unrelated pages without checking in first.

## Tab context and session startup

IMPORTANT: At the start of each browser automation session, call mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp first to get information about the user's current browser tabs. Use this context to understand what the user might want to work with before creating new tabs.

Never reuse tab IDs from a previous/other session. Follow these guidelines:
1. Only reuse an existing tab if the user explicitly asks to work with it
2. Otherwise, create a new tab with mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp
3. If a tool returns an error indicating the tab doesn't exist or is invalid, call tabs_context_mcp to get fresh tab IDs
4. When a tab is closed by the user or a navigation error occurs, call tabs_context_mcp to see what tabs are available

entries.description:
Use a mouse and keyboard to interact with a web browser, and take screenshots. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.
* Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element before moving the cursor.
* If you tried clicking on a program or link but it failed to load, even after waiting, try adjusting your click location so that the tip of the cursor visually falls on the element that you want to click.
* Make sure to click any buttons, links, icons, etc with the cursor tip in the center of the element. Don't click boxes on their edges unless asked.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported and will return an error - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels. Requires a Claude in Chrome extension version that supports scale; older extensions return the full-size image.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tabId.description: Tab ID to execute the action on. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

save_to_disk.description: For screenshot/zoom actions: save the image to disk so it can be attached to a message for the user. Returns the saved path in the tool result. Only set this when you intend to share the image — screenshots you're just looking at don't need saving.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__find
entries.description: Find elements on the page using natural language. Can search for elements by their purpose (e.g., "search bar", "login button") or by text content (e.g., "organic mango product"). Returns up to 20 matching elements with references that can be used with other tools. If more than 20 matches exist, you'll be notified to use a more specific query. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.

query.description: Natural language description of what to find (e.g., "search bar", "add to cart button", "product title containing organic")

tabId.description: Tab ID to search in. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__get_page_text
entries.description: Extract raw text content from the page, prioritizing article content. Ideal for reading articles, blog posts, or other text-heavy pages. Returns plain text without HTML formatting. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.

tabId.description: Tab ID to extract text from. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__javascript_tool
entries.description: Execute JavaScript code in the context of the current page. The code runs in the page's context and can interact with the DOM, window object, and page variables. Returns the result of the last expression or any thrown errors. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.

text.description: The JavaScript code to execute. Evaluated in the page context with REPL semantics: top-level `await` works, and the result of the last expression is returned automatically — write the expression you want (e.g. `window.myData.value`, or `await fetch(url).then(r=>r.json())`) rather than `return ...`. You can access and modify the DOM, call page functions, and interact with page variables.

tabId.description: Tab ID to execute the code in. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate
entries.description: Navigate to a URL, or go forward/back in browser history. tabId may be omitted for URL navigation when calling navigate STANDALONE (not inside browser_batch): tabs_context_mcp{createIfEmpty:true} is called for you and the first tab in the session's group is navigated — its result is appended to this call's output so you have the tab list and ids for subsequent calls. Inside browser_batch, navigate (and other tools that act on a page) requires an explicit tabId. Pass an explicit tabId when you need a specific tab or when the session's group has multiple tabs whose state you must preserve. tabId is required for url:"back"/"forward". A tab opened for you this way is yours to clean up, the same as one from tabs_create_mcp: close it with tabs_close_mcp once you no longer need it and before finishing your task, unless the user asked to see it or wants it kept open.

url.description: The URL to navigate to. Can be provided with or without protocol (defaults to https://). Use "forward" to go forward in history or "back" to go back in history.

tabId.description: Tab ID to navigate. Must be a tab in the current group. If omitted for URL navigation when calling navigate standalone, tabs_context_mcp{createIfEmpty:true} is called for you. Required for url:"back"/"forward" and for navigate (and other tools that act on a page) inside browser_batch.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page
entries.description: Get an accessibility tree representation of elements on the page. By default returns all elements including non-visible ones. Output is limited to 50000 characters by default. If the output exceeds this limit it is truncated at a line boundary, with a note giving the full size — pass a larger max_chars, or use depth/ref_id to focus on part of the page. Optionally filter for only interactive elements. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.

filter.description: Filter elements: "interactive" for buttons/links/inputs only, "all" for all elements including non-visible ones (default: all elements)

tabId.description: Tab ID to read from. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

depth.description: Maximum depth of the tree to traverse (default: 15). Use a smaller depth if output is too large.

ref_id.description: Reference ID of a parent element to read. Will return the specified element and all its children. Use this to focus on a specific part of the page when output is too large.

max_chars.description: Maximum characters for output (default: 50000). Set to a higher value if your client can handle large outputs.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp
entries.description: Close a tab in the MCP tab group by its ID. Use to clean up tabs you're done with. Only tabs in this session's group are closable; call tabs_context_mcp first to get valid IDs. If you close the group's last tab, Chrome auto-removes the group — the next tabs_context_mcp with createIfEmpty starts fresh.

tabId.description: The ID of the tab to close. Must be in this session's tab group. Get valid IDs from tabs_context_mcp.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp
entries.description: Get context information about the current MCP tab group. Returns all tab IDs inside the group if it exists. CRITICAL: You must get the context at least once before using other browser automation tools so you know what tabs exist. Each new conversation should create its own new tab (using tabs_create_mcp) rather than reusing existing tabs, unless the user explicitly asks to use an existing tab.

createIfEmpty.description: Creates a new MCP tab group if none exists, creates a new Window with a new tab group containing an empty tab (which can be used for this conversation). If a MCP tab group already exists, this parameter has no effect.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp
entries.description: Creates a new empty tab in the MCP tab group. CRITICAL: You must get the context using tabs_context_mcp at least once before using other browser automation tools so you know what tabs exist. Tabs you create are yours to clean up: close each one with tabs_close_mcp as soon as you no longer need it, and close any that remain before finishing your task. Leave a tab open only if the user asked to see it or wants it kept open.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__browser_batch
entries.description: Execute a sequence of browser tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — if an action navigates to a domain without permission, the next item's check fails and the batch stops. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested.

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, tabs_create_mcp). browser_batch cannot be nested.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","coordinate":[100,200],"tabId":123}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello","tabId":123}},{"name":"navigate","input":{"url":"https://example.com","tabId":123}}]

content.text:
All the code from Part II of the playbook is written and committed in 6 commits on `main`. Nothing is pushed yet. None of it has run against real Gemma, Atlas or Telegram yet, because there's no `.env`.

**What I checked:**
- The project typechecks cleanly. `mastra build` and `mastra dev` both serve `/`, `/try`, `/p/:id` and `/health`.
- `npm run test:workflow` runs the real workflow on the local Temporal server with mocked activities and compressed timers. All 9 checks pass: lock on the most-voted option, two failed weather calls then a retry that succeeds, no-quorum, rain fallback, and "Can't make it" never counting as a yes.
- The Temporal worker bundles under ESM, so the CommonJS fallback isn't needed.
- I reviewed the plan page and `/try` in your browser with fake data and fixed a timeline bug I found.

**Changes from the spec skeleton:**
- **Overpass was down everywhere I tried today.** Place lookup now tries mirrors, then Photon (also OSM data, but weaker names), and caches results in Atlas. Run `npm run places` once Overpass is up so drafts never wait on it.
- **Invented places are dropped.** Every draft checks Gemma's place names against the real place list and drops invented ones. If fewer than 2 real options are left, code builds them from real places.
- **Drafts get longer timeouts** (90 s for the request, 150 s for the activity). A Gemma draft with tools can take longer than 25 s. The weather re-check keeps a short 30 s timeout so Render's cold start still shows up as a retry.
- **The workflow carries on when retries run out.** If drafting fails, it tells the group. If the weather check fails, it keeps the plan and says the forecast is unknown.
- **The public plan page shows only vote counts by default.** Names appear only with `PUBLIC_NAMES=on`.

I didn't use your browser to create accounts or API keys. I'm not allowed to create accounts, and making keys or tokens changes your account settings, which needs your yes for each one.

**What you need to do:**
1. **Get keys:** a Google AI Studio API key, an Atlas M0 cluster (Network Access `0.0.0.0/0`), a Telegram bot from @BotFather (leave privacy mode on and don't make it an admin), and a Render account.
2. **Fill in `.env`:** `cp .env.example .env`, then add the keys, `HOME_LAT`, `HOME_LON` and `QUORUM_SHARED_SECRET` (make one with `openssl rand -hex 24`).
3. **Run Gate 1:** `npm run smoke` (20 drafts). If fewer than 16 pass, set `TOOL_MODE=prefetch` in `.env` and on Render.
4. **Cache places:** `npm run places`.
5. **Push and deploy:** `git push`, then on Render choose New → Blueprint → this repo and set the secret env vars. Put the `onrender.com` URL in `.env` as both `RENDER_URL` and `PUBLIC_URL`, and check that `/health` returns 200.
6. **Start the laptop side:** the Temporal dev server is already running in the background from my tests (UI on :8233); after a reboot, start it with `./scripts/run-local.sh`. Then run `npm run worker` and `npm run bot`.
7. **Test in a group:** `/join`, `/me no car`, then `/plan test`. That's a full run in about 10 minutes.
8. **Before the real run:** `git tag real-run-start && git push --tags`, then `/plan 2026-10-11 4`. Don't edit `src/temporal/workflows.ts` after the tag.

If you add the Google key to `.env` and tell me, I'll run Gate 1 and fix whatever it shows.

content.text:
The bot now runs on Discord instead of Telegram. It's committed (`f5abefa`) and nothing is pushed yet. The typecheck is clean and the workflow test still passes 9/9. With a fake token the bot gets as far as Discord rejecting the login, which is as far as I can test without a real token.

**How it works on Discord:**
- **Commands:** `/join`, `/me limit:…`, `/mine`, `/forget`, `/plan date:2026-10-11 people:4` (or `date:test`), `/status`, `/cancel`, `/recap line:… photo:…`, `/help`.
- **Poll:** a multi-select menu under the options message: pick every option you can make, or "Can't make it". The vote count on the message updates live, and each voter gets a private "Got it, you picked: …". I didn't use Discord's native polls because they cut answers off at 55 characters.
- **Recap:** the recap message has an **Add my recap** button that opens a text box, or people use `/recap` to attach a photo.
- **Privacy:** the bot asks for no privileged access, so it never sees normal messages, only slash commands and taps on its own buttons. That's Discord's version of Telegram's privacy mode.
- **One channel per group:** the roster and plans belong to the channel where people `/join`.
- **Optional ping:** set `DISCORD_PING_ROLE` and the 06:00 reminder pings that role.

**Bug fixed along the way:** the old bot would have refused every `/plan test`. Its "poll closes too soon" check required at least 10 minutes, but a test poll closes after 3. The limit is now 2 minutes.

**What you need to do now (instead of the Telegram steps):**
1. Go to discord.com/developers/applications, create a New Application, open **Bot**, and click Reset Token. Put the token in `.env` as `DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN`. Leave all the privileged intent switches off.
2. In Discord, turn on Settings → Advanced → Developer Mode. Right-click your server, choose Copy Server ID, and put it in `.env` as `DISCORD_GUILD_ID` so the slash commands appear straight away.
3. Run `npm run bot`. It prints an invite link; open it and add the bot to your server.
4. The rest of the earlier list is unchanged (Gemma key, Atlas, `npm run smoke`, Render deploy, `git tag real-run-start` before the real run). The test in a group is now `/join`, `/me limit:no car`, `/plan date:test`.

Your playbook's post draft and demo script still say Telegram, so the write-up will need to say Discord. I haven't touched the playbook.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

One real draft for Islamabad went through the same route Temporal calls, and it worked in 83 s: 2 tool calls, 2 options at real places (Kachnar Park, F-11/2 Park), each listing the roster limits that shaped it, 0 invented places, no fallback.

**Done since you added the keys:**
- **Atlas:** the login was failing because the password in `MONGODB_URI` still had the `< >` from Atlas's template. I removed them; your original `.env` is backed up in my scratchpad. Atlas now connects, and the vector index for semantic recall is ready.
- **Gate 1 passed.** Results are saved in `docs/evidence/gemma-smoke.md` for the write-up:

| Model | Valid with tool calls | Invented places | Median time | API errors retried |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gemma 4 26B | 8/8 | 0 | 128 s | 0 |
| Gemma 4 31B | 7/8 | 0 | 202 s | 4 |

  I made 26B the default, with tools called by Gemma itself (`TOOL_MODE=native`). Having code fetch the tools instead wasn't faster (120–193 s), so the time is in Gemma itself.
- **Timeouts:** drafts take minutes on the free tier, so draft and recap calls now wait up to 5 minutes. The original 90 s would have killed every real draft.
- **Places:** Overpass was down all day. Place lookup now falls back to Nominatim, which finds Margalla Hills National Park, Shakarparian and Rawal Lake Viewpoint. Results are cached in Atlas.
- **Discord:** with your OK I authorized the bot into your "quorum" server. It's online as `quorum#1044` with its slash commands.
- **Code:** everything is pushed to GitHub, and the workflow test still passes 9/9.

**Running right now, in my session:** the Temporal server, the worker, the bot, and the agent server on `localhost:4111`. The agent server stands in for Render until it's deployed, which also means `/p/` links in Discord only open on this laptop for now. These stop when this session ends, so for the weekend run them in your own terminals.

**What only you can do:**
1. **Test in Discord now:** run `/join`, `/me limit:no car`, then `/plan date:test people:1`. Options take about 2 minutes, then the poll appears; pick one, and the reminder and recap steps follow over the next ~8 minutes. I didn't type these myself because that would be sending messages as you.
2. **Render:** log in at dashboard.render.com, then New → Blueprint → `ArqamWaheed/quorum`. When it asks for secrets, paste `GOOGLE_API_KEY`, `MONGODB_URI` and `QUORUM_SHARED_SECRET` from your `.env`. I'm not allowed to type keys into web forms. Once `https://<name>.onrender.com/health` returns 200, tell me and I'll switch `RENDER_URL` and `PUBLIC_URL` over and check the deploy.
3. **Before the real run:** `git tag real-run-start && git push --tags`, then `/plan date:2026-10-11 people:4`.
